_why: The phrase a source comment uses instead of a chapter number. Feature 045, FR-008.
KEYED BY SLUG AND NOT BY NUMBER, because the number is the thing being retired. A slug
survives a reorder; an ordinal is a position, and chapter 3.7 recorded what happens to
one: 'A chapter number in a source comment is a reference that ages every time the plan
changes... The subject does not move; the ordinal does.'
IT SERVES ~605 REFERENCES, NOT 923. The other ~757 are provenance tags that delete and
consult no table — '(chapter 3.2)' at the end of a sentence, '// Chapter 3.8: nor the
notification relay'. Only possessives and subjects of verbs need a name.
THESE PHRASES ARE PERMANENT. They go into platform source comments and stay there, so
they are worth arguing about before ~605 substitutions are made. Each is a definite noun
phrase that reads in the middle of a sentence: 'the membership chapter's finding',
'the rate-limit chapter built'. A title would not — 'The words somebody wants back's
_review: DRAFTED, NOT SETTLED. Two entries are worth a second opinion before they are spent:
'the isolation gauntlet' and 'the outsider milestone' are the only two that do not end
in 'chapter'. Both are milestones and both already have names the book uses in prose,
so calling them chapters would read worse than naming the thing.
'the deduplication chapter' names the mechanism where the chapter title names the
insight ('Commit and publish are two instants'). Every comment citing it is about the
high-water mark, so the mechanism is what a reader of the comment wants.
AND ONE COLLISION WAS AVOIDED DELIBERATELY. Chapters 3.13 and 3.15 are both about
channels — the endpoints and the control surface — so they take 'channel-endpoints' and
'channel-control' rather than both becoming 'the channel chapter'.
